passage: Nirmala, come sit. Your mother says the stream form is due Friday and you can't sleep. Let me tell you about your uncle Gurpreet at sixteen. I had no idea what I wanted, and the deadline made my stomach flip every night. So I tried small experiments. One Saturday I sat in a print shop watching how jobs were quoted. Another day I asked our neighbour, a surveyor, what his week really looked like, the dull parts too. I picked commerce with a shrug, not certainty. At eighteen I moved to design, and nothing fell apart. The first choice was only a first choice. This weekend, go and ask someone with a real job what they do all day.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do one Saturday as an experiment?
qa.a: Gurpreet sat in a print shop watching how jobs were quoted.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling at sixteen, and what showed it?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt panicky and lost; the stomach flipping every night at the deadline and having no idea what to want show it.

qa.q: What small experiment could Nirmala try this weekend?
qa.a: Ask someone with a real job what they do all day, dull parts included, as Gurpreet asked the surveyor.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel on hearing that a first choice can change?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less pressured, since "the first choice was only a first choice" and Gurpreet moved to design at eighteen without things falling apart.

grounding: Gurpreet recalls fear at not knowing what to choose before a deadline, and small experiments, talking to real workers and revising later.

passage:
Tanvir, you keep saying you're the only one who doesn't know what you want. Come, sit with your Zeenat Phuppo. I was exactly like you at fifteen.

The stream form was due in ten days, and I couldn't sleep. Everyone around me seemed so sure: this one a doctor, that one a lawyer. I cried in the bathroom so Abba wouldn't hear.

Your grandfather's friend ran a pharmacy, so I spent four afternoons there, counting tablets and watching him talk to patients. Then I spent a Saturday with the librarian at our school. I asked a nurse at the dispensary what her day looked like, the boring parts too.

I picked science, mostly because I liked the pharmacy. Two years later I switched to library science for my degree. Everyone said I'd wasted time. I hadn't. The first choice was just the first one.

That's the only thing I want you to hear. Try a few things. Ask real people. Choose, and let yourself change.

qa.q: How many afternoons did young Zeenat spend at the pharmacy?
qa.a: She spent four afternoons at the pharmacy.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat feeling as the stream deadline came closer?
qa.a: She felt panicked and lost, unable to sleep and crying in the bathroom because everyone else seemed so sure.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped her most, and why?
qa.a: Trying the pharmacy and the library and asking people about real jobs helped, because it gave her real experience instead of guesses under panic.

qa.q: What was it like for Zeenat when people said she had wasted time by switching?
qa.a: It probably stung, but she did not see it as waste, since the first choice helped her find the second.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling panic at a stream deadline without knowing what she wanted, and how small experiments, talking to people in real jobs and revising the first choice helped.

passage:
Two days till the stream form was due, and the power had been out in Nikita's colony since noon. No laptop, no internet, just a torch and a phone at thirty per cent.

"I don't know what I want," Nikita said, pacing. "What if I pick wrong and ruin everything?"

Her friend Dolma, sitting cross-legged on the bed, said, "Then use the phone for something useful. Call people who actually do the jobs."

So Nikita did. Her aunt, a bank officer: "Numbers every day. Stable. Sometimes dull." Her neighbour's son, a lab technician: "Long hours standing. I like it." Her old tuition teacher, now a counsellor: "You can switch in Class 12 or after, Nikita. People do."

Battery at eight per cent, she wrote on the back of a notebook: commerce, try the school's economics club, check again after the half-yearly exams.

"It's not forever," Dolma said. "It's just next."

Nikita breathed out for the first time all day.

qa.q: How much charge did Nikita's phone have at the start?
qa.a: The phone was at thirty per cent.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she paced the room?
qa.a: Nikita felt panicked and afraid of picking wrong and ruining everything.

qa.q: What did Nikita do that helped her decide?
qa.a: Nikita called three people in real jobs, noted what they said, and made a choice with a plan to check again after the half-yearly exams.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Nikita's decision?
qa.a: Dolma sees it as a next step, not a forever choice, and wants Nikita to stop treating it as a trap.

grounding: It shows a teen who panics at a stream deadline without knowing what she wants, and calms by talking to people in real jobs and accepting that the choice can be revised.
